opus-5.5.text:
Oh, it's a little embarrassing, but I really am picky about it. For me, doing mathematics is very physical. When I'm stuck on a problem, I'm not sitting there typing. I'm scribbling, crossing things out, drawing little diagrams in the margins, and the tools either get out of the way or they get in the way.

With paper, I like something thick and smooth enough that the pencil glides, but with a bit of texture so you feel some resistance. If the paper is too thin you see the ghost of the last page through it, and that's distracting when you're trying to keep a clean picture of an argument in your head. With pencils, I like a softer lead, because you can write fast and lightly when you're exploring, then press harder when something feels true and you want to commit to it. And I like being able to erase. So much of math is being wrong, and I want being wrong to feel cheap and easy, not like a permanent ink stain.

There's also a ritual to it. Sitting down with a fresh sheet and a sharpened pencil tells my brain we're doing serious thinking now. It's a bit like an athlete with their particular shoes. The shoes don't win the race, but they take away one small source of friction, so all your attention can go to the problem.

And honestly, I think it comes from loving the subject. When you care deeply about something, you start caring about the small textures around it too. The pencil and paper are part of how I experience mathematics. It's where the ideas first become real.

r001.rationale: The response says a fresh sheet and sharpened pencil signal serious thinking and describes drawing while working, but it does not clearly state that good tools inspire a desire to draw.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's less about superstition and more about friction. When I'm working on a problem, the bottleneck is almost never how fast I can write, it's how long I can stay inside the problem without getting pulled out of it. Anything that snags my attention, a pen that skips, paper where the ink bleeds through so I can't flip back and read what I did yesterday, that's a tiny interruption, and the interruptions compound. Math thinking is fragile. You hold five or six things in your head at once and you're trying to see how they fit, and if the physical layer makes any noise, you lose one of them.

So I ended up with a few habits. I like paper that's slightly off-white and has a faint grid, because a grid lets me line up equations and draw diagrams without the lines fighting me, but it's quiet enough that it disappears. I write with pencil, not pen, because I want to be able to cross out and redraw freely. A lot of mathematics is just drawing the wrong picture four times until the right one shows up, and I don't want to feel precious about any single attempt. And I keep everything in bound notebooks instead of loose sheets, dated, because a surprising amount of my progress comes from going back and seeing an idea I abandoned two months ago that suddenly makes sense in a new context.

There's also something I'd say is almost about respect for the work. When I was a kid competing in olympiads, I noticed the people I admired treated their scratch paper carefully, not because it was going to be graded, but because the care on the page reflected the care in their thinking. Messy handwriting is fine, I have messy handwriting. But a messy process, where you can't trace how you got somewhere, that's where errors hide. So the tools are really just a way of making my own reasoning legible to myself. If I can read it back cleanly, I can check it, and if I can check it, I can trust it.

r001.rationale: The response says pencil and faint-grid paper make it easier to draw and redraw diagrams, but does not state that good pencil and blank paper inspire a desire to draw while doing mathematics.

astra-6.text: I think the physical experience of doing mathematics matters. You spend so much time writing things down, crossing them out, and trying again that the feel of the pencil on the paper becomes part of how you think. If it feels comfortable, I can forget about the tools and concentrate on the problem. And there’s a simple pleasure in using materials you like—it makes you want to sit down and work.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the physical experience of doing mathematics matters. I like being able to write smoothly, sketch something, erase it, and try again without thinking about the tools. When the pencil and paper feel right, they fade into the background, and I can focus on the problem. There’s also something comforting about that little ritual when you’re sitting with a difficult question for a long time.
